items.text: To address this, CiteSee provides a personalized research paper reading experience by automatically identifying and resolving inline citations in PDFs to research paper entities in our academic graph [50], and visually augmenting inline citations based on their connections to the current reader.
items.why: Explains how CiteSee resolves and visually augments citations.
items.plain: CiteSee matches inline citations in Portable Document Formats to paper entities in an academic graph and visually alters those citations based on how they connect to the current reader.

items.text: Using this signal, Cite- See scores and highlights inline citations to help the reader triage them and discover prior work that are likely relevant to their literature review topics (Figure 2).
items.why: Describes the short-term interest scoring mechanism of CiteSee.
items.plain: CiteSee scores and highlights citations based on a reader's recent reading history to help them discover relevant prior work.

items.text: Second, CiteSee leverages research papers saved in the reader’s Semantic Scholar paper library and the reader’s publication record [50] to understand their longer-term research interests.
items.why: Describes the long-term interest tracking input of CiteSee.
items.plain: CiteSee uses papers saved in a user's library and their publication history to track their long-term research interests.

items.text: In order to produce these annotations automatically, CiteRead first filters citing research papers for ones that are most relevant to the reader using a trained model atop a number of features representing citational discourse and textual similarity, i.e. from scientific paper embeddings [20].
items.why: Explains the filtering and modeling pipeline behind CiteRead.
items.plain: CiteRead uses a trained model to filter citing papers for relevance using textual similarity embeddings and citational discourse features.

items.text: CiteRead then localizes citing papers to particular spans of text in the paper being read, and extracts relevant information from the citing paper.
items.why: Explains how CiteRead places citing commentary into paper text.
items.plain: CiteRead locates specific text spans in the active paper and extracts relevant commentary from citing papers to present as margin notes.

items.text: a technical challenge because while inline citations reference cited papers, they do not typically reference specific locations in the cited paper; CiteRead determines location by looking for overlapping spans of text (e.g., a number in common in the citing paper and the cited paper) or localizes to the relevant section when this overlap is unavailable.
items.why: Details how CiteRead handles text localization challenges.
items.plain: CiteRead aligns citing papers to specific locations by finding overlapping text spans or by matching relevant sections.

items.text: Because readers often skim for common types of information, Scim uses a pretrained language model [99] to classify salient sentences within papers into one of four information facets: research objectives, novel aspects of the research, methodology, and results, coupled with heuristics that ensure an even distribution of highlights.
items.why: Explains Scim's ML model and heuristics for highlights.
items.plain: Scim uses a pretrained language model to classify key sentences into four categories—objectives, novelty, methodology, and results—and applies rules to spread highlights evenly.

items.text: Ocean [75] minimizes scrolling requirements for low-vision readers by providing bi-directional, viewport-preserving hyperlinks that enable navigating to and from associated content without disrupting the viewport.
items.why: Explains how Ocean reduces scrolling for low-vision users.
items.plain: Ocean provides bidirectional hyperlinks that jump between linked content without changing the visible viewport size.

items.text: Since papers do not always provide hyperlinks and automated link creation is imperfect, Ocean includes an authoring interface that allows readers to create and share paper links during reading.
items.why: Describes Ocean's authoring feature for manual links.
items.plain: Ocean includes an interface that lets readers create and share manually added links within papers.

items.text: First, it aims to reduce distraction by showing definitions with high economy: glosses show multiple definitions and and in-context usages within a compact tooltip.
items.why: Explains ScholarPhi's design for concise definition tooltips.
items.plain: ScholarPhi displays multiple definitions and in-context uses together in a compact tooltip.

items.text: Second, it provides position-sensitive definitions, revealing definitions that appears most recently prior to the selected usages of terms.
items.why: Explains ScholarPhi's position-sensitive definition selection.
items.plain: ScholarPhi shows definitions that appear most recently prior to selected uses of a term.

items.text: Terms and definitions are automatically identified using a pretrained language model [42].
items.why: Identifies the underlying model used in ScholarPhi.
items.plain: ScholarPhi automatically identifies terms and definitions using a pretrained language model.

items.text: Readers can access definitions of both a symbol and the subsymbols it is made of through a multi-click, “drill-down” selection mechanism.
items.why: Describes ScholarPhi's drill-down selection mechanism.
items.plain: ScholarPhi provides a multi-click selection mechanism to let readers view definitions of both full symbols and their nested sub-symbols.

items.text: Furthermore, when a reader selects a formula, they can see definitions for all symbols at once, automatically placed adjacent to the symbols in the formula’s margins (see Figure 5).
items.why: Explains how ScholarPhi displays formula-wide definitions.
items.plain: Selecting a formula in ScholarPhi displays definitions for all component symbols side-by-side in the formula margins.

items.text: These summaries are generated by prompting a large language model with section text [10].
items.why: Explains how Paper Plain generates summaries.
items.plain: Paper Plain generates summaries by feeding section text to a large language model via prompts.

items.text: A sidebar containing questions a reader may have about the text (e.g., What did the paper find? or What were the limitations?) provides links into answering passages identified using a question-answering system [106] alongside their associated plain language summaries.
items.why: Describes Paper Plain's question-answering indexing feature.
items.plain: Paper Plain uses a question-answering system to link sidebar user questions directly to relevant text passages and plain language summaries.

items.text: To grant authors more control over how their work is presented, we developed an AIsupported authoring interface for linking paper passages and videos efficiently: candidate passages are linked to excerpts of videos as suggestions using a pretrained language model [100], and an author interactively confirms or refines them.
items.why: Explains Papeo's video-text linking pipeline.
items.plain: Papeo suggests links between paper passages and video excerpts using a pretrained language model, which authors then confirm or adjust.

items.text: Using Threddy, readers can select and save sentences into a sidebar from the related work sections of a paper.
items.why: Describes how Threddy extracts text clips.
items.plain: Threddy lets readers save selected sentences from a paper's related work section into a sidebar.

items.text: The system maintains rich context for each clip, including its provenance and inline citations.
items.why: Explains the context tracked by Threddy.
items.plain: Threddy saves the origin paper and inline citations alongside each clipped sentence.

items.text: Finally, readers can further expand their coverage by exploring paper recommendations for each thread, based on the referenced papers in the corresponding clips.
items.why: Explains Threddy's paper recommendation mechanism.
items.plain: Threddy recommends additional papers for a topic thread based on citations included in saved clips.

items.text: Using a pretrained language model for summarization [56], Relatedly generates short and descriptive titles for each paragraph, and uses a diversitybased ranking algorithm so that the reader can quickly see and explore paragraphs describing different research threads, such as Fact Checking Datasets, Social Media and Misinformation, and Fake News Detection Techniques.
items.why: Explains how Relatedly generates titles and ranks paragraphs.
items.plain: Relatedly uses a summarization language model to generate paragraph titles and orders them using a diversity-based ranking algorithm.

items.text: Specifically, Relatedly dynamically re-ranks paragraphs and highlights sentences to spotlight unexplored and dissimilar references for breadth, but also allow
items.why: Explains Relatedly's dynamic re-ranking mechanism.
items.plain: Relatedly re-ranks paragraphs and highlights sentences to draw attention to unread references, while grouping paragraphs with similar citations together.

items.text: The SciA11y system6 demonstrates this approach, automatically converting 12M academic PDFs to HTML [97]; a user study with blind and low vision participants demonstrated strong user appreciation of the output, though some errors remain (e.g., failing in certain cases to distinguish footnotes from body text, difficulty parsing math equations) [98].
items.why: Describes SciA11y's implementation and evaluation.
items.plain: SciA11y automatically transformed 12 million academic PDF documents to HTML, which was well received by blind and low-vision participants despite minor parsing errors.
